verdict.headline: The Iran conflict reaches oil refineries, and futures price a cost shock rather than a crisis
verdict.label: Crude at six-week highs after strikes on Iranian tankers and Aramco's Jizan refinery; Dow futures -0.8% against -0.1% on the Nasdaq-100, the two-year yield unchanged at 4.381%, gold flat and the VIX near 15
verdict.rationale_short:
The weekend escalation crossed from shipping into energy production. US forces struck three Iranian tankers, one of them near Kharg Island, Iran's main export terminal; Houthi drones hit Saudi Aramco's Jizan refinery again; and Iran's parliament speaker warned that US oil and gas assets across the Gulf are exposed to retaliation. Crude rose for a third straight session to six-week highs, with Brent's November contract at $97.20 and WTI's October contract at $92.56.

The equity response is a rotation rather than a retreat. Dow futures fell 0.8% before the bell against 0.1% on the Nasdaq-100; energy shares rose, with Valero up 1.9%, Exxon Mobil 1.8% and Chevron 1.5%; and the four large US airlines fell between 0.5% and 2% after the IATA halved its 2026 industry profit forecast and put the sector's fuel bill at $350 billion. The largest premarket gain among the names moving was Eaton, up 3.1% on a UBS upgrade tied to datacenter demand, which is not an energy story at all.

The bond market says the same thing more precisely. The two-year yield was unchanged at 4.381% while the thirty-year rose two basis points to 5.271% and the ten-year sat at 4.806%, 1.2 basis points below the 4.818% level this report has tracked. A curve steepening with the front end pinned is an energy cost being priced, not a change in the expected policy path. The dollar index slipped toward 98.80, a two-week low, gold was roughly unchanged near $4,472 and the VIX sat near 15 — none of the three is behaving as it would in a genuine risk event, which is what locates the buying in oil specifically.

The target set is what changed since Monday. That report placed the shortage in refining capacity rather than in crude, and the weekend's strikes hit exactly that: Jizan is a 400,000-barrel-a-day refinery that shipped roughly 200,000 barrels a day of product in July before a July 25 strike shut it. Retail diesel reached $5.90 a gallon on September 6, above the $5.85 record set two days earlier, and freight sits in the cost base of most goods rather than in one sector — which is how a struck refinery arrives in Thursday's producer price print. A second cost landed the same morning: Canada's counter-tariffs on C$27.6 billion of US goods, more than 700 products at 15%, 25% and 50%, took effect at 12:01 AM across steel, appliances, agricultural equipment and electronics. Both shocks tax firms that move physical goods, which is what separates the Dow from the Nasdaq-100 this morning.

The evidence does not all point one way. Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast by $5 on Monday, and the new number, $85, still sits well below Tuesday's $97.20 — the sell side is treating this as a risk premium that decays rather than a lasting shortage, and a Hormuz transit agreement would take that premium out of crude without adding a barrel of refining capacity. The Asian memory bid that led Monday's session also failed to survive it: the Nikkei fell 1.7% to 65,269.33 and the Kospi 0.6% to 6,954.52, giving back most of Monday's gains on a broker inventory estimate nothing has since confirmed, and the Kospi has still never closed above 7,000.

Four thresholds now sit within roughly 1.5% of being crossed: 4.818% on the ten-year, 5.30% on the thirty-year, $95 on WTI and $78,000 on bitcoin, which is trading $218 above it. Three of the four are pushed by the same input. WTI through $95 alongside the ten-year through 4.818% would say energy is now setting the long end and the cost read has become a rates problem; the ten-year going through alone would point at supply and this week's Treasury buyback operations instead. A New York Fed one-year inflation expectations print at or below the prior 3.6% at 10:00 AM would say the pass-through is still confined to producers.
verdict.lede_short: The weekend's escalation moved from shipping to energy production: US strikes on Iranian tankers, Houthi drones on Aramco's Jizan refinery, and an Iranian warning that Gulf energy assets are exposed. Crude rose a third session to six-week highs, but Dow futures fell 0.8% against 0.1% on the Nasdaq-100, the two-year yield did not move and gold was flat — a cost being priced, not a crisis. WTI at $95 and the ten-year at 4.818% are what would change that.

watchlist_mentions.note: Fell with United, American and Southwest in a 0.5% to 2% premarket range after the IATA halved its 2026 industry profit forecast and put the sector's fuel bill at $350 billion. Jet fuel is a middle distillate produced from the same constrained capacity as diesel, so a Hormuz transit agreement that lowered crude would not on its own relieve this. The read that separates the two is whether the diesel crack holds above $100 while Brent falls.

WTI's October contract traded at $92.56, up 1.07% and a third straight session of gains, after US forces struck three Iranian tankers including one near Kharg Island and Houthi drones hit Aramco's Jizan refinery. $95 remains the regime threshold, 2.6% away. Goldman's raised December Brent forecast of $85 sits below spot, which is the sell side pricing a premium that decays rather than a shortage that persists.

Closed 0.6% lower at 6,954.52, giving back part of Monday's 4.61% rise, while the Nikkei fell 1.7% to 65,269.33. Monday's move rested on a KB Securities estimate putting memory inventories below ten days of supply; nothing has since confirmed it, and the index has still never closed above 7,000. Micron's next quarterly report remains the first company data able to test the estimate.

Trading at $78,218 on Crypto.com late in the European morning, down 1.51% over 24 hours in a $78,158 to $79,646 range and $218 above the $78,000 downside reference. A fifth session below $80,000, and it has not taken a bid from the energy escalation in either direction, which is consistent with the flat gold price rather than with a risk event.

trade_setups.asset: The split between firms that move physical goods and firms that do not
trade_setups.thesis: Two cost shocks landed on the same morning and both fall on physical logistics rather than on demand. Retail diesel set a second consecutive record at $5.90 a gallon, and Canada's counter-tariffs on C$27.6 billion of US goods took effect at 12:01 AM across steel, appliances, agricultural equipment and electronics. The premarket separation matches: Dow futures down 0.8% against 0.1% on the Nasdaq-100, airlines down 0.5% to 2% on the IATA's halved profit forecast, and the largest single gain an industrial with datacenter exposure, Eaton, up 3.1% on a UBS upgrade.
trade_setups.entry: The Dow-to-Nasdaq-100 gap is the measure of whether this is a cost rotation or the start of a broad de-rating. 7,700 on the S&P 500 sits 19 points below the September 4 cash close of 7,718.60.
trade_setups.invalidation: The Nasdaq-100 joining the decline at similar magnitude would say the market is selling equity risk rather than repricing input costs. Energy giving back its premarket gains intraday would say the same from the other side.
trade_setups.horizon: Tuesday, and into Thursday's producer price print

trade_setups.asset: WTI at $95 and the ten-year at 4.818%
trade_setups.thesis: Both thresholds are close and the same escalation would break both: WTI's October contract at $92.56 is 2.6% away, and the ten-year at 4.806% is 1.2 basis points away, with the thirty-year at 5.271% and 5.30% a further 2.9 basis points beyond. Iran has threatened a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf and warned that US energy infrastructure in the region is exposed. The two-year at an unchanged 4.381% is what currently distinguishes an energy cost from a policy repricing.
trade_setups.entry: $95 on WTI and 4.818% on the ten-year are the levels. Breaking together would say energy is setting the long end; the ten-year going through alone would point at supply and the Treasury long-dated buyback operations beginning Wednesday.
trade_setups.invalidation: A Hormuz transit agreement, which Iran said last week was in its final stages, would take the premium out of crude without adding refining capacity — crude retreating while the diesel crack holds would separate the two stories rather than resolve them.

trade_setups.asset: Whether the fuel move has reached household inflation expectations
trade_setups.thesis: The New York Fed's one-year consumer inflation expectations series prints at 10:00 AM ET against a prior 3.6%, and retail fuel is the most visible price in the economy: diesel at $5.90 a gallon and gasoline near $4.15 going into Labor Day. Producer prices follow on Thursday and consumer prices on Friday, with the FOMC in blackout through September 17 and hike odds for the September 15-16 meeting near 59%, so no official can frame any of the three before the decision.
trade_setups.entry: 3.6% is the prior. A print at or below it says the pass-through is still confined to producers; a move above it is the first evidence the pump has reached the household survey ahead of the official inflation data.
trade_setups.invalidation: A producer price print at or below July's 4.7% on Thursday despite record diesel would say the freight pass-through is slower than the refining margin implies, and would leave the August payrolls print as the only hawkish input still standing.
trade_setups.horizon: Today through Friday's CPI, into the September 15-16 FOMC
